title: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
hook: morning, afternoon, evening, Shabbat, festivals: the prayer book is a map of time
tomorrow: Elul: the king in the field

segments.voice: Yesterday, any language: the Shema, the Amidah and the grace, valid in words you understand. Your line was God understands every language. Which language did your thank-you come out in? Today, we close the prayer book. Day six hundred forty-one.

Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, we opened a book. A siddur. The word means order. For a hundred and four days we've walked it, roughly in the order it's prayed. Through the morning blessings and the rooster. The warm-up psalms. The Shema with a hand over the eyes. The Amidah on your feet. Kaddish, Aleinu, the afternoon pause, the evening's shelter. Shabbat welcomed like a bride. The festivals, the Days of Awe, and this last week, the prayers that live outside the book.
screen: `A BOOK CALLED ORDER.` → `A HUNDRED AND FOUR DAYS.` → `FROM THE ROOSTER TO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Step back and look at the whole siddur, and you notice it isn't really organized by topic. It's organized by time. It's a map of the clock and the calendar. Morning, afternoon, evening: three services a day. The Talmud links them to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And the book of Genesis gives Isaac a beautiful moment for the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." A psalm names all three times in a row: "Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and He hath heard my voice." Then the week: six weekdays with their requests, and Shabbat, when the requests go quiet and the Amidah becomes one long breath of holiness. Then the month, with the new moon. Then the year: the festivals with Hallel, the Days of Awe with their own thick book. Then a life: a prayer for a journey, a blessing after food, the Kaddish after a death. Open the siddur anywhere and the first question it answers is: what time is it? That's the deep idea. Prayer in this tradition isn't mainly something you do when you feel like it. It's a rhythm laid over time, so that the day itself has a shape. The day wakes into thanks. It pauses in the middle. It lies down into shelter. The prayers come back around, again and again, until the day is held by them, the way a riverbank holds the river. Tomorrow we turn from the book to the year itself, beginning with Elul.
screen: `ORGANIZED BY TIME, NOT TOPIC.` · `MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING.` · `THE WEEK, THE MONTH, THE YEAR.` · `WHAT TIME IS IT?` · then, large: `PRAYER SHAPES THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one prayer to keep. Look back over the whole walk: the morning blessings, the rooster's understanding, the Shema, the Amidah's open my lips, Birkat HaMazon, the evening's spread over us, the traveler's prayer, five words for someone sick. Which one stayed with you? Pick one. Decide when in your day it will live: morning, midday, meal, night. If you pray, say it now, once, slowly. If not, say the line you chose as a line to live by. The bell holds the time.
Siddur. Order: the prayer book's name, read today as a map of time, day, week, month, year and a life.
Your line: prayer shapes the day. Today, put your one chosen prayer at its time, and let it mark that hour. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Observant Jews pray three services daily, Shacharit, Mincha and Maariv, with added prayers for Shabbat, the new moon and festivals, all laid out in the siddur; many others keep one or two prayers, like Modeh Ani or the Shema at bedtime.
